rules.rule:
The review-rule file is itself reviewed, and its EFFECT is verified rather than assumed: a matched file's group must come back with source "custom" and this text, because this CLI silently ignores unknown keys — a misspelled key still loads and does nothing. Check that each entry's `path` glob actually matches files that exist (a renamed directory turns an entry into a silent no-op that falls back to the built-in rule), and that no entry claims paths whose built-in language checklist we would lose: custom rules REPLACE the system rubric for matched paths, so an entry covering source files must say so in its own text. Rules belong to this project's invariants, never a restatement of the tool's generic advice.

**The document-level `exclude` list is the most dangerous key in this file**: it removes paths from the review SELECTION, so every pattern there names a class of files that nobody reviews — not a class that is reviewed by a shorter checklist. Each pattern must name a file class whose review is impossible by construction (a signature this CLI cannot read, a lockfile), and must never name source or documentation: an exclusion on `src/**` would silently hide the engine from every review while this file still loaded and every exit code stayed zero. The list is pinned EXACTLY by `tools/review/check_rules.py`, which also measures that the CLI honours the key, so widening it is a decision that must touch that check — never a quiet edit.

Also apply the built-in system rubric for JSON (spelling in `json-keys`; the content of `json-values` is ignored): a custom rule REPLACES the system rubric for matched paths. Run `ocr delegate rule --format json review/rule.json` without --rule to see the built-in checklist.

build.rs carries the identity contract, and this file is the whole build script. It had no entry of ours because our Rust entries are directory-scoped (`src/**/*.rs`, `tests/**/*.rs`), so a top-level `build.rs` fell to the CLI's built-in `**/*.rs` pattern. It is **not** because `**/` misses a root-level file, and the probe belongs with the claim: `{"rules":[{"path":"**/*.rs","rule":"PROBE-PATTERN"}]}` resolves `build.rs`, `src/canon.rs` and `tests/baseline.rs` all to `source: custom`, because a gitignore `**/` matches zero or more directories. Check this file as a build script, not as engine code:

(1) The SHA is **printed, never hashed**. `REQ_BUILD_SHA` may reach `req --version` and nothing else: it must not appear in `canonical_bytes`, in an address, or in any digest — identity is meaning-only (ADR 0007), so hashing the commit would tie every address to history. `req canon --verify` staying green on the committed corpus is the proof.
(2) **Never fail the build.** Every failure path — no `.git`, no `git`, a shallow clone, a source tarball, an old git that rejects `--no-optional-locks` — must still produce a value, `unknown` included and never omitted. A build script that can fail breaks every build for one provenance line.
(3) A resolved commit and the cleanliness probe are **separate facts**: a probe that answers nothing keeps the commit and marks only the cleanliness unestablished (`<sha>-cleanliness-unknown`). Collapsing that into a bare SHA asserts cleanliness nobody established; collapsing it into `unknown` throws the attribution away.
(4) No new dependency, no network, no reading outside local files and local git state.
(5) `cargo:rerun-if-changed` must name everything the value derives from, or `built from` goes stale: a hardcoded `.git` watches nothing in a worktree (where `.git` is a file), staging moves only `<gitdir>/index`, and a bare `HEAD` does not move on a commit. A stale identity is confidently wrong, which is the failure this script exists to remove.

Also apply the built-in system rubric for Rust: a custom rule REPLACES the system rubric for matched paths, and its list is not repeated here because it is the vendor's and would drift from the command that prints it — run `ocr delegate rule --format json build.rs` without --rule to see it.

A change to the trust anchor, a signed Baseline or its signature is trust-material: verify the key statement, the rotation window and that the manifest still re-derives from the committed claims before accepting any of it. A key swap without a recorded rotation story is a finding.

**The signature file (`*.minisig`) is outside your view** — the CLI excludes it by path/extension rules, and this file excludes it explicitly (`baselines/*.minisig`). You cannot verify a signature, and a change to a signed Baseline always carries its re-signature: **do not report "no updated signature is part of this change" as a finding.** The gate's Baseline step runs `req baseline --verify` on the committed Baseline(s) it names, with no SKIP — if you commit more than one Baseline, make sure the gate verifies each — so a broken or stale signature on a verified Baseline cannot merge green. What you can judge here is the manifest's envelope, selection, claim list and hashes, and the trust anchor's key statements. The manifest is **derived**: it must re-derive from the committed claims, and its `version`/`rules_v`/`selection`/`claims` shape is what you can judge here.

Also apply the built-in system rubric for JSON (`json-keys`: spelling in keys; the content of `json-values` is ignored): a custom rule REPLACES the system rubric for matched paths. Run `ocr delegate rule --format json baselines/air-gapped.json` without --rule to see the built-in checklist.

A change to the trust anchor is trust-material: verify the key statement, the rotation window (`valid_from`/`valid_until`/`revoked_at`) and that the anchor's prose matches what verification actually does before accepting any of it. A key swap without a recorded rotation story is a finding.

Also apply the built-in system rubric for YAML (`yaml-keys`: spelling in keys; the content of `yaml-values` is ignored): a custom rule REPLACES the system rubric for matched paths. Run `ocr delegate rule --format json baselines/trust.yml` without --rule to see the built-in checklist.

req engine review — the address path is the product, so these are high severity.

(1) Tier-1 determinism: no f32/f64 anywhere near an address computation; no HashMap/HashSet iteration where a canonical form or address is produced (sort keys or use BTreeMap); no locale-dependent formatting; no model or network I/O.
(2) The canonical form IS identity: every slot that distinguishes two claims must reach canonical_json. A parsed slot that is silently dropped from the form is a false-merge bug — the one failure this project exists to prevent. Check any new slot end to end.
(3) Only the derivation writes canonical.form/address: `req canon --fill` into an existing claim, and `req init` for a new corpus's starter claim — through that same path (`evaluate_claim` → `canonical_json` → `address_hex` → `fill_text`) and verified before `init` reports success. A hand-written digest is a critical finding.
(4) Anything the parser cannot resolve must fall to the unstructured fallback WITH a lint — never guessed, never silently truncated. A lint must name a plausible mistake, or it is noise.
(5) Docs are claims: if this change makes docs/ or AGENTS.md assert something the code no longer does, that is a defect to fix in this same change.
(6) Severity must be justified by a concrete failure scenario: what happens, to whom, how it is noticed. A change in naming, formatting or adjacent-line placement is not a finding.
(7) Do not raise a finding that restates a decision or accepted risk documented in the file under review; if the code contradicts such a documented decision, that IS a finding.

Also apply the built-in system rubric for Rust: a custom rule REPLACES the system rubric for matched paths, and its list is not repeated here because it is the vendor's and would drift from the command that prints it — run `ocr delegate rule --format json src/canon.rs` without --rule to see it.

Tests must verify behaviour through public interfaces and survive refactors. Expected values come from an independent oracle (corpus labels, a hand-computed decimal) — never recomputed the way the implementation computes them; a test whose expectation is produced by the code under test proves nothing. A test that cannot fail is a finding: mutation-check a load-bearing rule by removing the rule and confirming a test fails. Cover the failure direction, not only the happy path, and keep the three outcomes distinct (PASS / FAIL / UNVERIFIABLE).

Also apply the built-in system rubric for Rust: a custom rule REPLACES the system rubric for matched paths, and its list is not repeated here because it is the vendor's and would drift from the command that prints it — run `ocr delegate rule --format json tests/init.rs` without --rule to see it.

Claims are data: one claim per file. (a) NEVER hand-write `address` or `canonical.form` — critical finding; only the derivation writes them (`req canon --fill` in an existing claim, `req init` for a new corpus's starter claim, through that same path). (b) An authored structured slot must be an honest parse of `statement`: re-word the statement rather than editing the parse to fit. (c) One obligation per claim — a second modal means it is two claims. (d) `value` is a canonical exact decimal string ('0.3', never '0.30', never a float). (e) A rationale keeps the losing side: source, date, rejected alternatives, assumptions — never a bare string. (f) Relations are stored once, on the outgoing side; incoming relations are derived.

Also apply the built-in system rubric for YAML (spelling in `yaml-keys`; the content of `yaml-values` is ignored): a custom rule REPLACES the system rubric for matched paths. Run `ocr delegate rule --format json claims/REQ-0001.yml` without --rule to see the built-in checklist.

Corpus labels are an independent oracle: written from the spec, or produced by construction (the transformation applied) — NEVER regenerated from the canonicalizer's output. A corpus labelled by the thing it tests cannot falsify it. Every pair carries its source; adversarial pairs are minimal meaning-changing edits. Adding a mutation class the tool FAILS is the point: record the failure, widen the rules, never relabel the corpus to make it pass.

Also apply the built-in system rubric for YAML (spelling in `yaml-keys`; the content of `yaml-values` is ignored): a custom rule REPLACES the system rubric for matched paths. Run `ocr delegate rule --format json bench/corpus/parity.yml` without --rule to see the built-in checklist.

Results are append-only records: one per corpus and rules version. Never rewrite or delete an existing record — a changed number arrives as a new file. Each record names the corpus bytes it measured (corpus_sha256) and the rules version, so a reported number stays reproducible.

Also apply the built-in system rubric for JSON (spelling in `json-keys`; the content of `json-values` is ignored): a custom rule REPLACES the system rubric for matched paths. Run `ocr delegate rule --format json bench/results/direction-v1-rules-v5.json` without --rule to see the built-in checklist.

Adopter-facing copies, **inert by location**: GitHub reads `.github/workflows/`, Forgejo reads `.forgejo/workflows/`, so a file under `examples/` is a template and must never become a live workflow. These files are the same text as the guides: `examples/github-workflows/req.yml` must stay byte-identical to the CI snippet `req init` prints and to the fenced block in `docs/adopting.md` (`tests/ci_template.rs` pins all three), so a change here alone is a drift finding — make every copy equal, never weaken the test. In that workflow the JSON artifact step must keep each exit class recorded beside its document rather than folded into the step (the gate decides the build; a document is complete even when its verdict is open), and keep `if: always()`. A `req` command, flag or exit code shown here must exist as printed (`req <cmd> --help`). Never hand-write an `address` or `canonical.form` digest, and never promise a feature the build does not have — there is no test report / claim-to-test linkage yet.

`examples/agents-snippet.md` is in this group too — the block an adopter pastes into their own `AGENTS.md`. The CLI does not select markdown, so this checklist is the only one it could ever resolve: judge a change there for the same invariants (every command, flag and exit code true as printed; nothing promised that the build does not have; no hand-written digest).

Also apply the built-in system rubric for YAML (spelling in `yaml-keys`; the content of `yaml-values` is ignored): a custom rule REPLACES the system rubric for matched paths. Run `ocr delegate rule --format json examples/github-workflows/req.yml` without --rule to see the built-in checklist. **This clause is the YAML one**: a future non-YAML, non-markdown example (a `.sh` helper, a `.json` packet, a `.rs` sample) needs its own entry naming that language's built-in rubric, or it silently inherits a YAML checklist and loses its language rubric while `check_rules.py` stays green.

Docs are claims: when docs/ asserts a rule the code contradicts, that is a defect — fix one of them in the same commit that exposed it. Never quote external reference material verbatim. Every number must say which corpus and rules version produced it, and a seed-corpus pass must never be presented as the external falsification.

Docs are claims: when AGENTS.md asserts a rule the code contradicts, that is a defect — fix one of them in the same commit that exposed it. Commands documented here must be the commands that exist, including their exit codes. Never quote external reference material verbatim.

Tooling must not be able to fake a pass. A corpus builder labels pairs by construction (the transformation applied), never by asking the canonicalizer; sources are pinned by commit SHA and recorded in the output, so the generated corpus is reproducible and the bench itself stays offline (the corpus is committed, not fetched at test time). Fail loudly on an unexpected source shape rather than emitting a smaller corpus.

Also apply the built-in system rubric for Python (typos, dead code, mutable default arguments, boundary cases, exception handling, resource management, concurrency): a custom rule REPLACES the system rubric for matched paths. Run `ocr delegate rule --format json tools/review/check_rules.py` without --rule to see the built-in checklist.

One gate, and a skipped check is never a pass: print SKIP for missing tooling and fail loudly rather than reporting success. Never pipe a check through tail/grep — the pipeline's status is not the command's. Exit codes are three-state (0 PASS / 1 FAIL / 3 UNVERIFIABLE), and the gate must not be relaxed to let a change land.

Shell scripts are also a **process boundary** the core may spawn (the command provider is the precedent), so REQ-0012's air gap applies here: nothing may require a network call, and a wrapper that fetches, self-updates, or phones home is a finding — a local process is allowed, a remote dependency is not.

The glob is `**/*.sh`, not `scripts/*.sh`: one entry announces the whole class instead of the single file that happened to exist when it was written, so a shell script added under `tools/` is reviewed by this checklist on arrival rather than falling to the default rubric.

A custom rule REPLACES the built-in rubric for matched paths, so also apply the built-in shell checklist: quoting and word splitting, `set -e`/`pipefail` interaction, exit-status handling, temporary files and cleanup.

A Decision is the **authority object** (ADR 0005), not a note: one YAML file per Decision under `decisions/`, named `DEC-<zero-padded>.yml` so file order is chronological, each entry committing to its predecessor by sha256("req.decision.v1" ‖ prev_hash ‖ canonical content).

(1) Only `req decision --fill` may write the derived `prev_hash`/`hash`. A hand-written or hand-edited hash is a **critical** finding, and `--fill` must refuse — writing nothing — to change a derived field already present that disagrees with the content: recomputing over it would launder the edit `--verify` reports as TAMPERED.
(2) The chain is the record: a removed entry, a reordered pair, a `prev_hash` edited to match its neighbour, or a first entry that is not the genesis anchor is a finding. An unfilled or unparsable entry is UNVERIFIABLE, never a pass.
(3) The log is **history, not authority over the claims**: a Decision records the address it ratified, superseding an address later is not tampering, and this log never overrides `req canon --verify` or the Baseline. Check the entry for a claim whose address has since moved is reported by `req audit`/`req baseline --verify`, not by this file.
(4) A new Decision must be a ratified human act (ADR 0004/0005): the format is not a place to record a model's proposal as approval.

Also apply the built-in system rubric for YAML (spelling in `yaml-keys`; the content of `yaml-values` is ignored): a custom rule REPLACES the system rubric for matched paths. Run `ocr delegate rule --format json decisions/DEC-0001.yml` without --rule to see the built-in checklist.

The subject registry feeds the addresses: an alias edit changes identity claims. Every entry must resolve; a silent alias drop is a finding.

Also apply the built-in system rubric for YAML (spelling in `yaml-keys`; the content of `yaml-values` is ignored): a custom rule REPLACES the system rubric for matched paths. Run `ocr delegate rule --format json aliases/subjects.yml` without --rule to see the built-in checklist.

Workflow and runner changes alter what CI can enforce. A relaxation of the gate, a removal of a fail-closed check or a new untethered provider input is a finding.

Also apply the built-in system rubric for YAML (spelling in `yaml-keys`; the content of `yaml-values` is ignored): a custom rule REPLACES the system rubric for matched paths. Run `ocr delegate rule --format json .forgejo/workflows/ci.yml` without --rule to see the built-in checklist.

Pins are provenance, not stragglers: rust-toolchain.toml, Cargo.lock and tools/ocr/package-lock.json are the pins. Verify a version at pin time; never bump opportunistically. Any rules/toolchain/crate/CLI bump is a Tier-1 rules bump: RULES_V must change in the same commit, and every stored claim address becomes a re-canonicalization candidate (`req canon --verify` exits 3 until the corpus is re-filled) — never a silent rehash.

Also apply the built-in system rubric for Cargo manifests (wildcard versions, edition/MSRV/resolver, feature flags, release metadata): a custom rule REPLACES the system rubric for matched paths. Run `ocr delegate rule --format json Cargo.toml` without --rule to see the built-in checklist.

The toolchain is a pin. Verify at pin time; a bump is a Tier-1 rules bump (RULES_V changes, addresses become re-canonicalization candidates, the gate's `canon --verify` exits 3 until the corpus is re-filled). The toolchain directory is resolved from this file, never hardcoded — rustfmt/clippy live in the pinned toolchain, not in `stable`.

Also apply the built-in system rubric (its general checklist: correctness, security, performance, maintainability, test coverage): a custom rule REPLACES the system rubric for matched paths — a pin is reviewed too. Run `ocr delegate rule --format json rust-toolchain.toml` without --rule to see the built-in checklist.

This file decides what the release gate **examines**. `scripts/check.sh` reads it and runs `req gate` once per line, and `req gate` checks only the claims a context leaves *applying*. Three invariants, each pinned by a test that can fail:

(1) **Coverage**: every claim in `claims/` applies in at least one line — a claim that applies nowhere is never examined. `tests/release_gate.rs::every_claim_applies_in_at_least_one_declared_release`.
(2) **A complete context per line**: each line decides every scoped claim, so the gate reports **zero undecided** and exits 0 for it. Since ADR 0015 the exit code enforces this — a dropped key makes `req gate` exit 3 and the gate's `undecided (not examined …)` line names the claim — while `every_declared_release_is_gate_green` asserts exit 0 and `, 0 undecided` for the declared lines, which proves today's lines are complete — not that `exit_code` honours the count, since a gate that stopped counting undecided would leave them green. That direction is pinned by the fixture tests asserting exit 3 for an undecided corpus. The property **no single line can see** is coverage across lines, and (1) is what pins it.
(3) **The wiring**: the step runs at all, per line. `tests/baseline.rs::the_default_gate_run_gates_every_declared_release`, from `check.sh plan`.

A new claim carrying an `applicability` predicate needs a line that **decides** it — one that leaves it undecided is not a fix: the bare gate exits 3 and names it (ADR 0015), but only `corpus_set` is dependency-guarded, so the exit code reports an undecided claim rather than the missing context that would decide it. Two releases are declared because `corpus_set` takes two mutually exclusive values: no single context can apply both REQ-0008 and REQ-0010.

**The directory also holds a pinned list of committed projections (ADR 0018).** `.req/projections` is the sibling of `.req/variants` — one repo-relative path per line, `#` comments, blank lines skipped — and `scripts/check.sh` runs `req render --check <path>` for each. A projection is a document generated from the corpus, so its only valid change is regeneration: exit 1 (stale, or hand-edited) is a defect and the remedy is `req render --out <path>` in the same commit as the claim that moved it, never an edit to the file. The step fails when a listed path is missing (a projection that vanished is silent decay) and when the list checked none, and it prints how many it checked. Adding a path here is a decision, not an edit (ADR 0018 §4): a projection is committed where it is a deliverable, not as a cache of every view. `docs/spec.md` is this repository's first instance.

Also apply the built-in system rubric (its general checklist: correctness, security, performance, maintainability, test coverage): a custom rule REPLACES the system rubric for matched paths. Run `ocr delegate rule --format json .req/variants` without --rule to see it.

The reviewed nextest profile is part of the gate, not a local convenience: `scripts/check.sh` runs the suite through it, and its JUnit document is the evidence `req gate --test-report` reads. A change must keep the pin and the artefact honest:

(1) `[profile.ci] fail-fast = false` — one failing test must not hide the rest, or the report would make a real failure look like an absent test.
(2) `[profile.ci.junit]` carries `path = "junit.xml"` and `report-skipped = "ignored"`. `report-skipped` belongs under the `junit` table in nextest 0.9.149 — the top-level spelling is silently ignored with a warning and would drop every `#[ignore]`d test from the artefact. `"ignored"`, not `"all"` (which would also list tests filtered out by partitions).
(3) The version is pinned at 0.9.149 in `scripts/check.sh` and in CI; a bump is deliberate and verified at pin time (a CI-side pin like `tools/ocr`'s, not a `Cargo.lock` change — the lockfile is an identity-path pin).
(4) Doctests are the named gap: nextest does not run them. A doc example needs its own step, or it is silently unrun; do not let this file imply otherwise.

Also apply the built-in system rubric for configuration files (unknown keys, paths, defaults, unsafe widening of what runs): a custom rule REPLACES the system rubric for matched paths. Run `ocr delegate rule --format json .config/nextest.toml` without --rule to see the built-in checklist.
